utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, the witness Dr. Ranta is here. She is a court witness, the first I think that we've had in this case, and therefore I will repeat the procedure so that the accused can hear it. When she has taken the declaration, I shall invite her, if she wishes, to add anything to her statement. After that, it will be for the Prosecution, who will have up to an hour to examine her. That will be followed by examination by the accused, again up to an hour. It doesn't have to be that long, but he will have an hour available. The amici can ask questions, if they so wish, at the end of that, and then the Judges will ask any questions which they wish to clarify matters at the end. But first we should begin by exhibiting her statement, which has not been exhibited yet, of course, together with the attachments to it, and I will invite the registry to give it a suitable number, court number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is Chamber Exhibit number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, before the witness comes in, --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Sorry. That will be -- for shorthand, it will be Exhibit C1. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before the witness comes in, I'm grateful to you for indicating the procedure to be adopted. It wasn't, of course, a matter of discussion, or arguments weren't advanced as to the appropriate procedure for court witnesses. May we reserve our position to make further arguments in relation to the appropriate order of questioning for perhaps other --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. If it's a matter of objection, now is the time to do it. That is the procedure which we have adopted with other court witnesses in other cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and I said I was going to reserve the position to make representations either in the case of this witness, if problems arise, or in relation to other witnesses if they have particular characteristics about them. Our concern, let me make it absolutely plain, is that with this witness, if there are matters that require what would be achieved by re-examination because, for example, there hasn't been a proper and full explanation of something, it won't be available to us. But my position is that we would seek to reserve our position to argue what may be the appropriate order of questioning witnesses, particularly with other witnesses whom the Chamber may call, and I reserve my position to make representations about the possibility of asking further questions at the end of the accused's questioning if it seems to us that things have not been left in a satisfactory position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, the normal course of events, the Prosecution should go first and the accused should have the opportunity of cross-examining. That must be the right order. If there are matters unexplored which you wish to have another go at, then of course you can make the application.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, is there anything you want to say about that procedure?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. In my view, you expressed it correctly as to the correct procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll have the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If the witness would take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Dr. Ranta, thank you for coming. Could we begin by your giving, for the record, your name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Mary Helena Ranta.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And briefly your present position and occupation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was originally trained dentist. Currently I hold a position of forensic odontologist at the Department of Forensic Medicine, University of Helsinki, Finland, and I'm a coordinator of the disaster victim identification activities at the national and international level, including also international missions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've asked you to come here in order to clarify various documents and statements which have been made, and let me tell you what the procedure will be. The first thing is that if you wish to add anything to your statement which we have, yourself at the beginning, of course you may do so. That will be followed by examination by the Prosecution. They have been told they've got up to one hour. Followed by examination by the accused, he having the same time. And sitting beside you are the friends of the Court, the amici. They may wish to ask some questions, and the Judges may wish to ask some questions at the end to clarify any matters which aren't clear. If at any stage you want to refer to any documents, of course do so. I notice you've got a binder there. Perhaps you could tell us what documents you're referring to when you do so we have it for the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will only refer at this stage to the documents which have been submitted by this Tribunal to me as annexes to its order dated in late January this year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. You may be asked about some other documents which will be put to you, but otherwise, of course refer to those documents you've brought. Now, the first thing is this: Do you want to add anything to what's in your statement? We've all had a copy, and we've had the opportunity to read it. It's a matter for you whether you want to add anything - sometimes witnesses do - or you may prefer simply to go straight into the examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think there's anything essentially I would like to add at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Nice. Questioned by Mr. Nice:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Ranta, if we can first just set the scene and then check on one or two things you've said and then check on the materials that have been available to you. You went into Racak how many days after the alleged killings had occurred?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: I did not go to Racak in January 1999. The first time I went to the village or in the vicinity of the village was -- well, I passed by car. I passed Racak, the village, in late January 1999, but physically I did not enter the village and did not visit the sites where the bodies had been recovered on 16 January 1999. The first time I was working at the village and conducting investigations at the village was in November 1999. I sent investigators of the European Union forensic expert team to visit the sites where the bodies had been recovered on January 30, 1999, but it had been snowing the previous night, so --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're going to have to use the time a little more efficiently. It's not your fault, it's mine entirely. How many days after the alleged killings were you first involved in examining the bodies?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: That is six days after --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: -- the recovery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By that stage, they'd already been examined to some degree by others?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: To my knowledge, 16 of them had been autopsied by local experts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The report prepared by those other experts was a report you were not prepared to sign; correct?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: No. No, we were not prepared.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In due course, a substantial report was prepared by yours -- by you and others, and that's part of the material that's been considered by this Tribunal through another witness, Dr. Baccard. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were then reported as having said one or two things of significance about Racak. First, it was reported that you had said -- I'll get the precise words. First it was reported that you had said at one stage the following: "You could say that the entire scene in the little valley had been staged. I am aware of that because this is actually a possibility. Our initial investigation results suggest this, as do the later forensic examinations we conducted on the spot in November 1999, and we forwarded this conclusion immediately to The Hague Tribunal." Do you remember saying something to that effect in a television interview?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: I remember saying, and I can recall that very clearly, that as a forensic scientist, at the very beginning of any investigations, you have to be open to all possibilities, and among these possibilities you always have the possibility of a setup. I can't recall saying that during the scene investigations that would have remained among the possibilities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By using the phrase "could have been staged," or, "the entire scene could have been staged," were you expressing anything more than the general, the philosophical possibility? Were you saying anything about the probability of it being staged on this particular occasion?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: I'm a scientist, and I have -- I had several hypotheses. I think it's very important to remember all possibilities. But when I said "could," I was not referring to any probability.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You subsequently were reported in a press article as saying the following - and Your Honours will find this in -- as an attachment to our motion to admit the documents of Dr. Ranta.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us make sure -- before we go on, let us identify it. Is this the --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Attached --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It seems to be undated and I haven't got the attachment, but it's an article beginning, "Somebody has to do this job."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Correct. And we go on from there one, two -- about three sheets to ERN number 03058902 at the top, and it's halfway down that page. And if we've got a spare copy, we can put it on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness should have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The witness should have it herself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, could you repeat the number of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. At the top right-hand corner, it's 03058902, if you've got the same bundle of documents.

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I have that page here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Then you were reported in a press article to this effect: "Thanks to on-site investigations and countless --" bottom of the screen. Thank you very much. "Thanks to on-site investigations and countless hours on the computer, she, that is Dr. Ranta, got all the facts. She now knows where the bullets were fired from, point blank, not, as the Serbs and Belorussians claim, from a distance of 200 metres. She knows how many weapons were fired, what kind of bullets were used, that the victims were shot in the clothes in which they were found, not in UCK uniforms, and that they were shot where they were found. Under the surface, investigators found a bullet along with fragments of human teeth. These tooth fragments were found to be missing from a corpse lying precisely in that location. The DNA was identical. "By the middle of 2001, Ranta had convincing proof that Racak had not been faked, but the German and French media continued to hypothesise a Western conspiracy. You can imagine this is you being quoted. You can imagine how I suffered, but I wouldn't say a word. I wouldn't influence the public." Now, Dr. Ranta, it's right, I think, that you have never been in contact with the team in the Office of the Prosecutor dealing with this accused, as a potential witness for the Prosecution, have you?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: No, no, I have -- I have only submitted the findings of our autopsy -- of -- from the autopsies I have submitted to the Presidency of the European Union and the results of the scene investigations have been submitted to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as I've explained, they've been used and presented. Your contacts with the team prosecuting this accused have, I think, been limited to probably telephone and then written contacts with an investigator called Curtis about this article from which I've just read an extract?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, Kevin Curtis contacted me in summer 2002 in reference to this article, and I wish to make a correction which I already did in my statement which was submitted in summer 2002, and there is and on the very page which you referred to, "by the middle of 2001." It is "by the middle of 2000" instead of 2001. And I made that correction in my statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I help you a little further, because having only that limited telephone and correspondence contact with Mr. Curtis, he wrote you a letter to inquire whether the newspaper article was correct. You replied to him by a letter of the 9th of August, 2002 - which perhaps that could be also displayed; it's the immediate following pages in the Court's papers - where you dealt with the article in a very detailed way, correcting indeed the reference to 2001. As to the body of the longer paragraph that I read out, paragraph 5, you said this: "The expression 'all the facts' --" this is at the bottom of the page, please, Usher. "The expression 'all the facts' would apparently indicate that the complete sequence of events on the 15th to the 16th of January, 1999, could have been established on the basis of recovered evidence. The approximate positions from where some of the bullets have been fired could be concluded as well as the minimum number of weapons used." And then you said, as to paragraph 6: "Should be 'By the middle of 2000.' On the basis of recovered and analysed materials, it was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. possible to conclude that the gully indeed was the site of the killings." So those were the only corrections you made, or qualifications you made to the newspaper article. May we take it that subject to those qualifications, you stand by the way you were reported in that article?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I wish to emphasise my first reference in this statement, and the interview was delineated to the gully and therefore my comments, and that this statement is restricted accordingly to cover the investigations. I'm not referring to all the developments in it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Quite right. But as to the gully, the way you were reported, subject to the qualifications expressed in the letter to Mr. Curtis, was accurate.

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again so that there can be no uncertainty or confusion, apart from that correspondence with those prosecuting this accused, you've had no contact with the Office of the Prosecutor since because you've been summoned here by the Court and not by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: I have had no comment -- no connection with --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Accordingly, there's been no session with any lawyer on the Prosecution side, and it hasn't been, in those circumstances, possible to explore with you other materials available to assist you in the conclusion that you've reached.

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: We have had no sessions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In those circumstances, help us, please, with this: Have you seen any contemporaneous photographs of the bodies found in the gully?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: I have -- we have used -- the European Union team has used the documentation of the OSCE as the basis for its investigations and also the scene investigations and the results, and the report only uses the documentation by the OSCE. I have seen lots of photographs, as I believe everyone in this room has seen, and I'm aware of extensive documentation by different parties of the bodies found at the gully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, before you leave the article, we ought to deal formally with it. We ought to exhibit it. Perhaps you could tell us where it's from. Remind us of that and give it a date.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. The article -- I'll just get the precise date of the article if I can. The article is published on the 7th of July of 2002 by Bernhard Odehnal in Weltwoche. Your Honour, of course the papers are before the Court as an annex to our application, but I can see that they do need to be separately exhibited, and it would perhaps be appropriate to exhibit the letter of the witness to Mr. Curtis together with the article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What we'll do is this: We'll give the article C2 and we'll have the letter C3.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour and the Court will recall that a considerable number of visual aids of one kind or another have been considered by the Chamber in relation to Racak, some of them at the hands of the accused in his cross-examination. It seems to me it would be helpful for this witness to have an opportunity to review at any event some of the photographs most considered by us, to check whether she has any comments to make on them, whether they would in any sense affect the conclusions that she's reached. May she have an opportunity to do that now, as the Court will realise that it hasn't been possible for us or proper for us to approach her before? They are to be found in the Racak volumes, number 1 of 5, with Exhibit number 156, and it's tab 5, and it may be, if the usher would help me, that we could simply display them fairly rapidly for the witness so that she could see then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have you any copies for her so she can have them in front of her or are you just relying on the one --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The one. We're going to rely on the Court's copy, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Dr. Ranta, you're going to be shown some photographs now. You'll be told what they are. You're going to be asked, I expect, your opinion about them. You haven't seen them before, so it will be a difficult exercise for you. If you can't, you don't think you can give an opinion, just say so and it will save time. But if you can, you think you can, then of course do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we have a look at tab 5, we can probably correlate them as we're going along. The first binder, tab 5, please. If there is any problem, I'll simply make mine available and I'll work from the screen. The better course is to use mine, and we'll locate them later. They're the photographs taken by Mr. Hendrie, if the Court recalls. We'll put them on the projector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll go through them quite swiftly, please, but you'll have an opportunity to see them in detail if you want to. That's a scene of the gully generally. Next, please. Further scene of the gully. Next, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Doctor, if at any time you want more time with a photograph, just say so. It's awkward anyway having to look at the side.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. If we can find another copy, we will. Next, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I won't ask you to trouble with that unless you want to, position of the bodies. Next, please. And Dr. Ranta, if you'd just look at them and indicate when you're happy to move on to the next one. While you're viewing them, do you recall seeing these documents before, yourself?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: I've seen some 30.000 photographs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: And I have to tell this Court that the faces of these people are very familiar to me. I know their clothing. So it's very difficult to say whether I have actually seen that particular photograph. I have seen photographs very similar to that. I can recognise the faces. I can recognise even the exit and entrance wounds, and I can recognise the missing parts of a human face. So -- but having seen that particular photograph, it's impossible for me to say. If I may continue. I have seen the drawings which are here as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we just go through them, please. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: If I am expected to say if I haven't seen one particular photograph, so the photograph 0072 -- 732330 I haven't seen before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: I haven't seen the following, the last three digits 331. I haven't seen 332.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: I haven't seen this particular photograph 333. The last three digits 339, 340, the top one and the lower magnification, I can't recall seeing this photograph before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: As well as 341, 342. The last three digits 348, with the belt. There are magnifications which I --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just that one, you see the one now on the screen at the moment? Have you seen this one before?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: I have seen this victim. I have seen photographs of this victim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we display 354 on the overhead projector, please. 354, 355. Have you seen that before or any other photograph of that victim?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: I can recall, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And then we can see on the following photograph, can we not, a view taken of the injury or wound to that man's, the previous man's, neck, which of course required some movement of his body in order that that picture could be taken; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we go back, please. I want to focus on this, Usher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you look at 32356, thank you. Dr. Ranta, in order to take this view of the man shown in the previous picture, 354 -- you can put 354 on -- it would have been necessary for the man's body, or head in any event, to have been moved to some degree in order to take that view of his neck.

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: I assume so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: But I wish to emphasise that according to the impression which I have and the members of my team have, so most of the bodies must have been turned around at some stage, which is a very natural reaction for someone who enters a scene like that. So probably if someone is facing the ground, people entering the scene would have a natural tendency, and it would be human, to turn the person around to see whether he or she was alive or whether he or she was someone he knew.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can move beyond that one. The next one, 357. Go through them swiftly. 358, if we can. 359, the wound. 360, 361.

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: 359 is a close-up, a detail which I haven't seen before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. 3 --

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: And the magnification 361.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. 362? 363, that is. 364, another photograph of the same.

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 365. 366 is another --

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: I haven't seen the 366.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then we can go on to 367, 368.

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: Again, 369 is not familiar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 369 is not familiar.

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: 369, this closer look at the site is not familiar. I can recall the autopsy findings, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 370 is currently on display. Then we go to 371. 372 comes next, further up the gully, I think. 373, 4, 5, and 6. 377 --

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: 376 I can't remember seeing, 376.

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: They're all familiar to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 380? And more lying as individuals, 381, 383, which we're up to there, I think.

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: They're all familiar to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 384, 385, 386 and 7, 388, 389. And then we come to these perhaps less significant, and we can stop here. We come to the first picture, I think, of someone in a house. And since we are concerned with the gully, I needn't trouble you any further. So, Dr. Ranta, thank you for that. I'm sorry it's taken some time, but it follows that the majority of the photographs that have been relied on by the Chamber thus far are either identical to or similar to photographs of these victims that you have seen before.

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And therefore, they are likenesses that you have taken into account in reaching the decision that you did eventually, as you made clear, to the effect that the killings occurred in the gully and that this was not a staged event.

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: My -- the results of the European Union team and which I referred -- which I have referred to is based on our scene investigations and the results of the scene investigations in relation to the autopsy findings. And as has been discussed earlier, one has -- had to bear in mind the possibility of a setup at the very beginning. So we adopted a very systematic scientific approach to test these different approaches, not just relying on sets of photographs, not --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no. I understand that. Dr. Ranta, there's no hint of criticism. I just need to be sure that included in the material that you relied on when following the careful process you've summarised were photographs of the kind or identical to those that have been considered by this Chamber, and the answer is that you did have such materials available to you.

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then I can be very brief, because time is limited. And you set out in your statement -- you set out in your statement and there is therefore no need for me to repeat particular features of your findings that confirm the fact that the bodies were killed where shown in these photographs; correct?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the Chamber or others can always ask you about those, if necessary. Now going back to look again at the history of the investigation that I summarised to you at the beginning. By the time of your arrival, most or many of the bodies had already been the subject of autopsy by the local personnel.

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: Sixteen autopsies had been conducted prior to our arrival to Pristina. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are aware of the suggestion that many of those bodies produced results positive to something called the paraffin test, although as we can find, I think, such findings were not actually recorded contemporaneously in their records, but that's another matter. The paraffin test was, at the time of this examination, already a very old if not out-of-date test. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, that was the first time in my professional career that I ever came across the practice of applying paraffin test to detect gunshot residues.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you conduct on the bodies you examined a different and more modern test?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: We were informed by Serb investigators that they had conducted paraffin tests prior to our arrival, and this was an information which I received in Pristina. Now, contrary to this information, among the documentation which was submitted by this Tribunal to me, there are several references that the paraffin tests were conducted in our presence and with the understanding of the European Union team, and this is not true. We were not present at the time when these paraffin casts were made, and we were not present either when any fingerprinting was conducted, and again, it has been claimed that this occurred in our presence. This is not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Back to the previous question, however. You conducted a different test to check whether any of the hands of those you were examining had been in contact with explosives or bullets or whatever else it is, and your test was entirely negative, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Prosecutor, but it would have been most unprofessional to conduct any gunshot residue testing on hands of the victims any more. We did not conduct them on hands.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: We took samples of selected clothing and some pieces of bone, but it would have been a waste of time and most unprofessional to do any -- any scanning electromicroscopy EDX testing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: These tests should be taken three to six -- within three to six hours after the alleged firing, not a week or two weeks afterwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, within the papers there may have been some ambiguity as to whether you did do these tests. You confirm that you did them, and you did them on clothing.

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: We did it on selected clothing and some separate bones, parts of bones. If I can remember correctly, it was a piece of a skull.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you found nothing to indicate contact of the kind revealed by this test?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: These tests were all negative. I -- and if I may continue. I think it is important to mention that we did conduct some testing because of the transparency of the work which we were doing in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One last question on this topic. The paraffin test was something you'd never seen or heard of being used. Just how out-of-date is it or how inappropriate is it as a test?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: I have heard that it has been used -- it was detected in 1930s, if I remember correctly. And just for the interest of -- of this Court, I could refer to textbooks from 1950, 1985, 1997, and 2000, and this test is mentioned here because of the historical value of the test, but it was abandoned already at the INTERPOL meeting in 1968, if I remember correctly, and it is of no scientific value because it does not indicate the presence of any gunshot residue specifically.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Moving perhaps chronologically through the process of your examination of the bodies and considerations of all the materials, just to summarise the position: From all the materials you found or heard of being found at the site, you found significance in the position of cartridge cases, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: We recovered both bullets, bullet fragments, and cartridge cases in the vicinity of the bodies, where the bodies had been found.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Spent cartridge cases being consistent with a number of locations being used to fire from; is that correct? Do I understand you correctly on that?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A concentration of bullets under bodies or under the -- at the places where bodies had been found being significant for the obvious reason that that indicated they'd been killed where they fell?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: I wish to emphasise the fact, Mr. Prosecutor, that the bullets and bullet fragments were recovered under the surface of the ground where the bodies had been recovered. So they have penetrated the ground, and the metal detectors which we used and applied in our investigations, they were adjusted to reach the depth of 30 centimetres. But due to the quality of the soil, most bullets were recovered in a depth of 3 to 5 centimetres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Some or it may be many of the bullets found had attached to them soft tissue remnants from bodies, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: They carried degrading soft tissue remnants.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that has an obvious significance to it.

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: We proceeded with extraction methods to get amplifiable DNA. Unfortunately, we failed, but there are scientifically applicable explanations for that failure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You saw nothing significant in the clothing or pattern of clothing worn by the individuals you examined?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: As a general comment, I would say that they were -- they wore several warm pullovers, and I assume that this was due to the fact that it was winter, and I assume that the heating was not appropriate at the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can be reminded that there were several elderly people included in those who were killed, and one woman.

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: I have no final information about how many people were killed on or around 15 January, but those -- my comments are restricted only to those 40 that were autopsied and among them there was one woman. All others were male, and among the males one was a boy, and there were several elderly people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the clothing, you found no evidence of military or paramilitary insignia having been removed.

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: No, we didn't find any, any indication of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And indeed, in short, you found nothing to indicate that these individuals were other than unarmed civilians.

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: At the time -- at that time, there was no indication of them being anything but unarmed civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're concerned now, of course, only with the bodies in the gully. There's been evidence given of activity elsewhere in the village and indeed the KLA commander at the time has been called to give evidence, so we've heard all about that. We're just concerned with the gully. I think you've explained this, but just in case there is any ambiguity, the bullets under the surface of the ground confirm that they fell where they were shot. The bullets penetrated the ground and stayed underneath the ground; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: That's my conclusion, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The entry and, where they existed, the exit wounds from firearm deaths were consistent entirely with these people being killed at close range or fairly close range?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: I wish to emphasise that I'm not an expert on ballistic, and in fact, I asked several experts on ballistics what they really consider a close range or short range, so the answers are very variable. So I think I refrain from any comment. I'm referring to the surveying of the gully.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Although difficult to express an opinion on this given the time at which you first saw the bodies and the fact that they were being removed, I think you are able to express a general opinion about the fact that they would appear all to have been killed at the same time.

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: The pathologists, regardless of whether they belong to the local expert team or to the European Union expert team came to the conclusion that they were killed approximately at the same time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the cold weather conditions at the time made it more possible to arrive at this sort of conclusion than would warm weather conditions?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: I wouldn't comment on that. What I would say only is that the fact that both the temperature at the gully, at the village mosque, and at the department -- at the Institute of Forensic Medicine University of Pristina was close to zero contributed to the preservation of the bodies so there were no considerable post-mortem changes detectable, which then made it easier for the pathologists to conduct their work.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that concludes all I need to ask the witness, given that her statement is in evidence and before you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Ranta.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Questioned by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I won't put questions to you as to whether these people were dead or not, because that is indisputable. Do you agree that the fundamental issue here is whether these people were killed in battle or whether they were civilians and whether they were killed on that spot or whether the whole group or part of the group was brought there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's not for the witness to say what the fundamental issues are. If you want to ask her about those questions, of course you can, but it's not for her to say what the issues are. That's for us to say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have -- I have nothing to add at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. On the 17th of March, 1990 [as interpreted], which is exactly a week before the beginning of the NATO aggression against Yugoslavia, in your report which you distributed to the journalists present at the press conference in the hall of the Assembly of Kosovo and Metohija, and this report was under an embargo until 1300 hours on that day, you wrote that this was your personal opinion and view of the events in Racak. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: First I would like to correct. The press conference was held on the 17th of March, 1999, not 1990. The press conference and the press release --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. 1999. There was an error in interpretation. I did say 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Just one thing. Have you got -- let's make sure we've all got the documents in front of us. There should be the press release, which is Annex 3 to your statement, Exhibit C1, embargo until 1300 hours, Pristina, 17th of March, 1999. That, I take it, is the press release to which reference is made. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. You were going to say about the press conference and the release.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This press release represents my personal view at the time it was released.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware at the time that your statement was being used as justification for the aggression that was to take place against Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That begs a question that it was being used. The witness can simply be asked this: Did you -- were you aware that any use at all was going to be made of your statement as has been suggested to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm only a forensic scientist and that's all. I don't know anything about the developments at the political level or other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But as a forensic scientist, you were at the head of a team, and I assume that the team finding was to have been communicated. Am I right in saying that you could not have had a team finding on which all the team members had agreed that would be identical with the opinion that you put forward?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: The team -- teams -- the results of the team's work were submitted as the final report on the autopsies, and everything that is in the autopsy reports is reflected also in -- in this press release.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, then. Tell me, why did you say that this was your personal opinion then?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: I have consulted experts on international law, and at that stage, the senior legal advisor of the European Union forensic expert team advised me to add this comment here. I understand that press releases of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. this kind usually have a reference like this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Mrs. Ranta, tell me, what does this political aspect you are now mentioning have to do with the forensic profession you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: I am a forensic scientist and I have no political affiliations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. But are you aware, Mrs. Ranta, that this statement of yours, whether it's your personal opinion or not, was used as an alibi to conduct an aggression against a country?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is not for the witness to say. It's merely your supposition. It's not for her to answer. Now, go on to something dealing with her evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is for her to answer whether she's aware of it or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. No, because the question you put forward is merely a supposition on your part, part of your case. It's not for her to say.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May. Then I'll put questions to you instead of her.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Ranta, in your report, you said that the references of the team of pathologists cover medical autopsies of only 40 victims brought to the hospital. Is that correct? Let's speed up, if possible.

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: Only 40 bodies were transported, according to the information which we received from different sources, from Racak to the Institute of Forensic Medicine, University of Pristina. I am not aware of the total number of casualties during the previous week, the Thursday, Friday, because we only came to the region the following week and started working together with Yugoslav and Belorussian experts on Thursday, that is, a week after.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Ranta, my time is very limited. This was a typical question that you can answer with only a yes or no. Please don't waste my time. In your report, you said that the findings were based on information originating from the bodies in the morgue and that you had no control over the bodies and that in the Racak case things that were indispensable had not been done or had been done improperly, and this refers to gathering evidence, localising the victims, finding gunshot residues, placing bodies in body bags, and so on, and that the medical investigation cannot answer the question as to whether there had been fighting or not. This is what you stated in your report. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: It is stated in the press release, and it can be found in the autopsy reports. The manner and cause of death, if it is possible to categorise those, is mentioned in each autopsy reports. So the cause of death is documented, and because at the time we had no further information about circumstances around death and no scene investigations had been conducted, the manner of death was left open.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But you say - this is on the page of your report that's marked as 223380: "Moreover, a medical investigation cannot give a conclusive answer to the question as to whether there had been fighting or whether the victims died under other circumstances." Here you expressed your personal opinion, as you say, and you say that the medical investigation cannot provide a conclusive answer as to whether there had been fighting or whether the victims died under other circumstances. Is this correct, Mrs. Ranta?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: Are you referring to the press release?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What are we referring to, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I've been sufficiently clear, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, you haven't, because nobody is following. So you're not clear. Just tell us what the document is and then we'll find it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the document that you have already identified, the press release, it's called Report of the Expert Team of Pathologists of the European Union on the Events in Racak, of the 17th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the aggression.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And the passage you referred to, what page is it of that document, because we don't all have the same numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, here it's on page 4 of this document, but their number is 223380.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, they may have those numbers, but we don't.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will lose a lot of time with this, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've been through it before; if you're going to put something to the witness, a passage, you must give her the chance of reading it. Now, is this the -- I'm looking at page 4 in our version is the last page. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in my set of documents it's five pages, details on the incidents in Racak. All this is in here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us go to this passage. Of course we're dealing with it in different versions it's probably the case, but on page 3 of the English, Doctor, the second paragraph begins: "The Racak events have been described as a massacre. However, such a conclusion doesn't fall within the context of the team..." et cetera. And then further down: "Moreover, medicolegal investigations cannot give a conclusive answer to the question of whether there was a battle or whether the victims died under some other circumstances. A full criminal investigation combined with interrogation of witnesses by appropriate investigative entities could shed more light..." et cetera. That appears to be the passage you're being asked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Mr. Milosevic, what do you want to put to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that you were engaged exclusively in your professional forensic work, no other kind of work. Here you stated your opinion: A medical investigation cannot give a conclusive answer to the question whether there was a battle or whether the victims died under some other circumstances. Is this your position and do you abide by it?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: I don't understand you. What kind of political aspect could be connected to this -- this sentence? There's no policy in this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not speaking of the political aspect. I'm just asking you whether as a medical expert dealing in nothing else, as you say about yourself, are you putting forward your purely professional opinion that a medical investigation cannot give a conclusive answer to the question whether there was a battle or whether the victims died under some other circumstances? Was this your position and do you hold the same position today?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: Medicolegal investigations as conducted by the European Union forensic expert team were at that time restricted to the medicolegal findings from the autopsies and the analysis of any evidence recovered during the autopsies. At the time of the press release, we had no other information about the -- these victims, these 40 victims that had been autopsied. So medicolegal investigation alone is not able to answer the questions like whether there was a battle or whether they died in other circumstances. There are other investigations needed to clarify these questions and, finally, it is the court that will then draw conclusions based on the evidence presented to it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Mrs. Ranta. In spite of what you have just said and in spite of your saying that medically you cannot establish whether there had been a battle, in spite of this, in your report you state that you cannot say whether there was a conflict or not, and yet you describe this as killings of unarmed civilians. How could you have said that these were killings of unarmed civilians when you could not have known this and when it was not your job to talk about this at all? Was this the alibi for the NATO aggression, for you to say that these were unarmed civilians?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. I've told you this witness is here as a scientist. She's given her answer as to that, and your putting forward your suppositions is not proper at this stage. Now, what's the question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question is just what you said, Mr. May. On the basis of what kind of science did Mrs. Ranta say that these were unarmed civilians on the 17th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness answer that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Referring to my press release, the text on the English version on page 3, I state: "There were no indications of the people being other than unarmed civilians." I didn't say anything more or anything less. No indication of the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Mrs. Ranta, it's quite clear. I mean, at a public press conference you said that these were unarmed civilians, and this was the alibi for the NATO aggression. Now, tell me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you're going to go on making speeches, I'm going to cut this short. You either ask this question -- you either ask this witness proper questions or you're stopped altogether. Now, if you've got any questions about her evidence, you can ask it, but making your speeches is simply not going to get us anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Ranta, you gave this conclusion, I'm reading from your report, on the basis of the fact that the people who had been killed were not wearing uniforms, they had no ammunition in their pockets. Did you know or do you know that many of your colleagues had opportunities to see many members of the terrorist organisation UCK who had been killed and who were wearing civilian clothes, wearing no uniforms or insignia, and most -- for the most part without UCK insignia? Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: I wish to ask the accused to be more precise when saying "your colleagues." Are you referring to the members of the European Union forensic expert team?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Specify what it is you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Many doctors, professionals, observers from the European Union and so on saw many members of the KLA who had been killed while not in uniform, and there is no doubt that they were members of the KLA, just as these people were. Do you think that if someone is not wearing a uniform they do not belong to the KLA?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: I ask the accused to be more precise, whether he's referring --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us deal with it in this way: First of all, he says there were reports, he says, by your colleagues, unspecified, that members of the KLA were found who were not in uniform. And then there's a second question: Do you think if someone isn't wearing a uniform they do not belong to the KLA? So there were two questions. The first question is: Did you know about reports of people being found who were members of the KLA who weren't in uniform? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wish to emphasise that there were no other forensic teams in the region at the time the European Union forensic expert team was established. So until 17 March 1999, I was not aware of any other forensic colleagues working in the region. So in that sense, my answer is no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. The next question: Do you think if someone isn't wearing a uniform they do not belong to the KLA? I.E., do they have to be wearing a uniform in order to belong to the KLA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not an expert on military questions to say that somebody is a member of some military affiliation as such without proper documentation is worthless. They cannot. Everything is possible. I'm not thinking that membership of any military affiliation. I'm more concerned whether people who were killed, whether at the time of their killing they fulfilled the status of civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's precisely the point, Mrs. Ranta. How could you have established then and stated that these were civilians? On the basis of the fact that they were not wearing uniforms? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: I said that there was no indication of them being anything but unarmed civilians, and this was based on the findings of their clothing and the findings of corresponding exit and entrance wounds in the clothing they were wearing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. In the report of March 1999, you also say that some bodies that were found in the mosque were not wearing any footwear, suggesting that the footwear had been removed out of custom. Is that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. correct? You say here: "The shoes of some of the victims seem to have been removed, probably before they were taken inside the mosque," and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's the first paragraph of page 3, please. "Shoes of some of the victims, however, had been taken off."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. This is correct. I have stated this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why were the shoes removed?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I could give several explanations to that, some of them more plausible than others. I am not aware of the religious tradition of these people. There could be one reason that, as I understand, you are not allowed to enter the mosque wearing shoes. There is another very understandable explanation as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: One explanation is that people were short of clothes and shoes, so they might have taken the shoes of those who didn't need them any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Ranta, isn't it logical, if this had been done out of religious custom, that all those carried into the mosque would have had their shoes taken off, not just a certain number of them? Isn't it logical that their shoes were taken off because they were wearing military boots? Doesn't it seem a possibility to you?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: I think that this question put forward by the accused can be actually answered by looking at the photographs from the sites of recovery of the bodies and comparing that with the findings of the autopsy reports and also with detailed photographs taken at the mosque. So I think based on this photographic comparison, which is very simple to do, one can conclude then whether that explanation put forward by the accused could be relevant or not. To my recollection, and I want to emphasise I don't know what is a military boot, but I can't recall of seeing any, any military boots that would resemble those, for instance, I have seen in Finland. They were more shoes of -- of simple winter shoes worn by people who live in the countryside in harsh conditions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Ranta, on all these photographs here, you have people wearing military boots. Here, have a look at them. And in the report of Professor Dunjic and other professors, expert witnesses, it says that they even have markings, a "O" signifying that they were made in Germany. And here, have a look at these photographs. There you can see the military boots.

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: Your Honour, based on these photographs, I'm unable to say that they are military boots.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Just for the record, we should be able to identify what these photographs are. Can the Prosecution help?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Ms. Graham says if you give us a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can have them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Did you get them, Mr. Milosevic, from the Prosecution papers, these photographs? Where did you get them from?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. They're all their photographs, all of them theirs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Hand them back. The witness says she can't help. We will identify as to whether they have been exhibited or not. If not, if you want them exhibited, we'll consider doing so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I add something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can remember that particular victim, and I remember that we have documented the clothing, including the shoes. So in the autopsy report I think there should be enough information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be we can turn that up in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: While we're finding the photograph reference, this is the first time that the accused has made reference to the documentation of someone else. It's one of the things I was concerned about right at the beginning of this morning's session. It's a reference to the report of Mr. Dunjic. The witness has not, of course, reviewed those documents for the reasons that have been made plain when I explored the limited nature of her contacts with the OTP. I don't press the issue on the Chamber, certainly not at this stage, but the Chamber may want to consider, if the accused is going to ask any further questions derived from those reports, whether she should be given an opportunity to read them in full.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This was a small point. We're not going to have the whole report exhibited on that point. And the accused is entitled to ask questions about it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we'll come to those reports too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Dr. Ranta, did you take a look at all of the photos that were shown to you or did you look at the first photo only?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll exhibit these if they haven't been exhibited already. Perhaps someone could find out over the adjournment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: They have been exhibited, we think, tab 7 in the first volume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Of 156, the registrar says. So we have them exhibited and they have now been referred to. So perhaps the accused can have those back.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May I just see them for interest?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, of course, and indeed the amici too should be able to see them. It's time for the adjournment. Dr. Ranta, would you help with one matter, which is this, that we've had references to a report of the 17th of March, 1999, and also references to the press release. Do we take it that in fact all there was that day was this press release, but for some reason it's occasionally been called your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is or has been considerable confusion about this. The report, as I see a report, that is the 40 autopsy reports submitted to parties, and the press release is just a press release, and there is no additional report, any secret report or anything like that, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll adjourn now for 20 minutes. Would you remember not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over, Dr. Ranta. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the photographs shown all come from Exhibit 156, binder 1, tab 7, or binder 2, which is the witness's report, which itself produces the photographs. Binder 2, tab 12. They are, if I may say so, selective, and by no means do they show all the pictures of all the feet, socks, shoes and otherwise. But those are the exhibit numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, before I continue, I hope that it is also clear to you that at this speed or at this rate or, rather, at this slow pace, I will not be able to get through my cross-examination of this witness with the limited time that I have been given, so I hope you're going to let me have a little more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Provided you make good use of the time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'll continue where you yourself left off, Mr. May, a moment ago, because you were insisting upon me explaining that on the 17th of March, 1999, it was not actually a report but that it was just an ordinary press release. And the witness herself said that it could not have been a report at that time, and that is something that is not being challenged at all. That is to say that she actually said that. And she also said that she had a legal advisor, senior legal advisor from the European Union who suggested to her that she write what she wrote in her report, that it was her own opinion, et cetera. Now, as this could not have been a report as such and as it was compiled with a great deal of attention with the advice of a legal advisor, why then does it say on it "Report of the Expert Team of Pathologists of the European Union About the Events in Racak," on the Racak incident. So if it was not a report, why does is say "Report of the EU Forensic Expert Team on the Racak Incident"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let's see what the report is. Yes. It's the heading of the press release is described as a report. Perhaps you could help.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, before going into the title of the press release, I wish to emphasise that I was not advised by any legal representative of the European Union. I was advised by the senior legal advisor of the European Union forensic expert team, who worked for the team. And going to the original question of the accused why it was titled report, because the report was submitted that very day, prior to the press conference, to Yugoslav authorities to the District Court of Pristina and this press conference was held afterwards. I'm sorry if there has been confusion about this press release being a report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Did you write the release yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How did it come about that you got this legal advice? Was it sought by you? How was it raised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wish to emphasise, Your Honour, that during the whole course of our mission in the region, already starting in mid-October 1998, I felt it appropriate of having a senior legal advisor as a member of the team. He never came physically to the region, but he worked together with us all this time. And I think it is very important, particularly when working out the legal framework of missions like this, to have legal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What I'm asking is can you give us the context in which you got the advice to say that this was your personal opinion? I mean, how did the discussion start? Was it something that you raised or was it something that he raised? In what context did it arise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was raised during our discussions, and I'm unable to say whether it was my own idea or whether it was an idea that came up during the discussions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then explain to me, please, if this was just talk with journalists, why your text is titled "Report," and why was it distributed prior to the press conference itself, the text that we have before us?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: This text was distributed during the press conference, and the report was submitted prior to the press conference, the report being the autopsy reports. And I already said that it is probably unfortunate to use the word "Report of the European Union Forensic Expert Team," when it's only a press release, but it was distributed at the press conference.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But are you aware -- very well. But are you aware of the extent to which the fact that you wrote the title as being "Report of the EU Forensic Expert Team" makes the contents far more serious, the contents contained on this piece of paper, and leads to certain conclusions and the creation of public opinion in general?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you think you can answer that, do. If you can't answer it, it may be just a comment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I'm allowed to explain in detail. Members of the forensic science community are not accustomed to dealing with representatives of media, and therefore I very reluctantly participated the whole press conference, and I wasn't at that time aware of the possible importance of how this paper would be entitled, whether that actually would play any role. To my opinion, it does not, and I think it is an oversimplification to pick up one single incident and focus on that when we are dealing with a series of tragic incidents. So focusing on only one incident, in this case the Racak, gives a wrong impression of the whole developments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Ranta, as you say that you don't give press statements, that it isn't customary and so on, do you allow then for the possibility that you were perhaps manipulated and the fact that this went under the title of the report bears that out and by placing you in the position of presenting that report at the press conference on the 17th of March? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: As I already stated before, I wrote the text of the press release myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is being suggested, and you should have the opportunity of answering it and dealing with the suggestion because it's a serious one for a scientist, is that you were being manipulated. It's not specified by who. But it's suggested that you in some way were being manipulated in writing this press release. Is there any truth in that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not at any stage during the preparation of this press release manipulated by anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you can help us if you're making a suggestion that this witness was being manipulated as to who it is that you say manipulated her so that she may understand fully what your suggestion is. Who do you say manipulated her?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it's like this: Do you remember that at the conference that the conference was attended by the officials of the European Union, for example, Gruber, the German ambassador, the Finnish human rights minister, Mr. Timo Lahelma, then there was the main individual of this manipulation, William Walker? I'm sure you'll remember that. So do you think and do you allow for the possibility of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One thing at a time. Was the press conference attended by those gentlemen?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: The press conference was attended by Ambassador Gruber, representing the Presidency of the European Union, by Ambassador Timo Lahelma, representing the Finnish Ministry for Foreign Affairs, and myself. We were sitting together, the three of us, at the podium. I was told afterwards that Ambassador William Walker was also present there, but I couldn't see him during the press conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You were told he was there but you didn't actually see him yourself. Fine. Now, why did the Yugoslav medical expert team, why was it made impossible for them to attend the press conference? I don't know the reasons why they did not attend the press conference too.

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not in a position of answering this kind of question, because I did not organise the press conference.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who did organise it then?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: This press conference was held at the OSCE headquarters, and it was organised as -- as I was informed, by the Presidency of the European Union in collaboration with the OSCE.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And with respect to that case, the incident, the press conference was attended by Ambassador Gruber of Germany but without the corresponding investigating judge and experts from Yugoslavia. How come that you as the head an institute did not present a single result from the post-mortems that are customary in cases of that kind and are presented in cases of that kind, and that is why in this report you use more a political terminology rather than professional scientific terminology? Why is that?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: I think there are now several -- several aspects which I have to -- have to make reference. I am not able to answer the question why the investigating judge or any representatives of the Yugoslav experts weren't present at the press conference. I wish to emphasise that they were the first ones to receive the report. Prior to the press conference, there was a submission of the report to the investigating judge, Danica Marinkovic, from the District Court of Pristina, and to the Institute of Forensic Medicine represented by Professor Dobricanin, who was the head of the institute. So they were the first to receive the report. And there was a question about why my report -- I use more political terminology rather than professional scientific terminology. My answer is that I had never thought of my terminology being political. This is the first time when I -- when I hear that. And there's not very much I can say to that. I was addressing the shortcomings in the procedures, investigative procedures. I am not aware of the political impact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're not aware that after that report came out, which as you say should not have been called a report, that seven days after that was when the aggression, NATO aggression against Yugoslavia started. So you don't consider that to be political?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's not for the witness. She can answer the questions, of course, about the press release, but she can't answer questions about the NATO intervention unless you're suggesting that she's in some way involved in it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Fine. Well, that's quite obvious, Mr. May, because it's all linked up. And it was used precisely to launch the NATO intervention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But you're not suggesting that this witness was in any way involved in the NATO intervention, are you? Because if you are, you should put it to her.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that is precisely what I'm claiming, because this is part --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Let us put that to the witness. What the accused suggests is that you were in some way involved in the NATO intervention which occurred sometime after this report. It seems to be suggested that there was a conspiracy, it seems to be what is being put, in which you were involved for NATO to intervene. Now, is there any truth in that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is no truth in that, and I wish to emphasise also the fact that the European Union team members were all of Finnish origin, Finnish nationals, and Finland is not a member of NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All the worse. But take a look at this piece of paper, please. The title of which, and I have received it with the documents, it says "Monitor, new doubts about the Racak massacre."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now just before we go any further, this is the document -- I'm grateful to Judge Kwon who has it. It's -- let me see. It's annexed to the report, Annex 4. Yes. We've got a translation somewhere. Let the witness have a copy of it if she hasn't already got one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The document you are looking at is the translation of the Annex 4 you presented.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, have it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have it in front of me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.
