utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, indicating this link, this connection which relates to the NATO aggression that followed, you can see what is quoted here. William Walker, the head of the OSCE mission, on page 2, that is, in his quotation, "It strengthened [in English] the opinion in Europe and North America as well as in the OSCE and European Union that something finally had to be done. It was the beginning of a process that eventually led to the bombing." [Interpretation] And then it -- the Monitor comments: "The dead were used, however, to silence misgivings about the sense of NATO attacks." Therefore, does this clearly speak about the links and ties involved?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm responsible only what I have investigated myself and reported myself and said myself. I'm not in a position of saying anything about William Walker's comments, why he chose to use what he said, and I'm not able to comment on the journalists' talks either. I only speak for myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But at the beginning of that same page, it says Dr. Helena Ranta, chief pathologist: "Racak was a KLA stronghold at the time. I am convinced there is enough information to suggest that there was fighting between the Serbian army and the KLA in the village. [In English] There is absolutely no doubt about that. I was also told, and was able to read reports that KLA fighters were killed that day." [Interpretation] And that's what you yourself said.

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: Yes, I have said that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then on that same page, it goes on to say, a statement by Zymer Lubovci, KLA member, who says the following: [In English] "We saw the Serbs coming, so we took up position and opened fire. We already --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness cannot comment on what somebody else said, the KLA member, but she can of course comment on what is attributed to herself. You accept, do you, that there was this interview with -- it was German television, was it? I may be reminded if I've got that right or wrong. Is this the transcript of a document or is it from a journal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a transcript of the interview given in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Although this does not relate to you yourself, it says here and you said a moment ago that you were informed about it and it is linked to what you claim, that as you yourself said, it was a KLA stronghold at that time. And they go on to quote Wayne Merry, former US government advisor: "There is no doubt that the KLA cynically calculated that loss of their own civilians and portraying them as victims world-wide was a condition for getting the West to intervene militarily."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. What do you want the witness to say about that? It's precisely the sort of question which I suspect she can't answer. This is all argument, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. If we can't have that, we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your findings, you speak about forensic expertise and the European Union team, forensic team. Dr. Ranta, is the truth quite the reverse, that you joined together with the Belorussian experts the Yugoslav group of experts composed of leading specialists from Yugoslavia, pursuant to orders issued by the competent investigating judge? Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: The European Union forensic expert team and in the capacity of team leader, I received already on Saturday, 16 January 1999, a phone call from Yugoslav Ambassador Mr. Crnogorcevic in Helsinki, asking us as a team to conduct the investigations. And upon our arrival, we were issued a court order by the District Court of Pristina specifying our position to investigate manner and cause of death, possible contributing factors to the death and circumstances around death, and finally, identification of victims. So we were working as an independent team in good collaboration with our Yugoslav and Belorussian colleagues.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ah, fine. So from what I can see here, you didn't have any comments with respect to the work of the experts from Yugoslavia. And in your first reactions after the post-mortems found in Racak, you say that there were no substantial differences in the findings and opinions between the pathologists of Yugoslavia and Finland. Isn't that right, Mrs. Ranta?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: I wish to emphasise that the professional work at the autopsy theatres was very smooth regardless of the national origin of the experts, and we were able to conduct the autopsies very smoothly and in a very good professional spirit. And this also extended to the forensic investigators.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there was no problem with respect to cooperation and collaboration. Why not then, if that was the case, did you not mention at the press conference or in the report, at least mention what your colleagues, members of the team stated and the facts that you were able to ascertain together, which is contrary to your claim that it was civilians who were involved, because your colleagues had occasion to see killed KLA fighters and very rarely came across uniformed persons. Usually they were persons who had no insignia or markings of any kind on them.

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: I wish the accused would be more precise in referring to the status of the victims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I'll come to that in due course, but first let's clear this up. Throughout the autopsies of the persons killed in Racak, was the representative of Finland for human rights present in the hall all the time, the First Secretary of the German embassy as well, a representative of the OSCE? Were they always present? I'm talking about the team, the Lahelma team, the First Secretary of the embassy Ottman, Michael Patterson, representative of the OSCE. Those are the individuals I mean. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: If we are talking about the first 16 autopsies that were conducted Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. prior to our arrival to the region, I'm not able to comment who were present and who were not. What I know is that Ambassador Lahelma was not there and I'm not aware of the presence of -- of who were present from the OSCE. If I can make right recollection of the first 16 autopsies, I believe that an OSCE officer called Eamon Smythe was present there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And now with respect to what you asked me, that is the specifications, you asked me to specify with respect to the claims made by your colleagues, that is to say persons who together with you conducted the autopsies and who present information and data on the basis of which the sole conclusion that cannot be drawn is that they were indeed civilians. Quite the contrary, the conclusion that can be drawn is that they were members of the KLA. For example, these were Professor Dunjic, Dobricanin, Tasic. You cooperated with them, did you not? So from the military boots, army boots with the "O", Austria, found on 23 individuals via the characteristic uniform or types of underclothes, the same type of underclothes, and the results of the paraffin tests which showed that 37 had shot from weapons, from firearms, 37 of the 40, according to the paraffin test results. 37 had shot from firearms. And in their reports, and I have their reports here before me, that means that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, we must have a question. Otherwise the witness is not going to be able to follow. What is the question for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From those reports, that is to say from the reports of individuals who cooperated and collaborated with you, was it clear that they were indeed members of the KLA and not civilians? And I have their reports here before me, both the report of Dunjic, Dobricanin, and Tasic, and these are their statements given to the opposite side over there. So these are not their personal private reports, nothing of that kind; they are the official reports given to the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us deal with these matters one by one. First of all for the witness: Do you know anything about these reports which have been referred to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have in front of me reports, 40 autopsy reports which have been most probably submitted to the investigative judge of the District Court of Pristina, Danica Marinkovic. With reference number KRI14/99. And there are altogether 40 autopsy reports. As I have already stated earlier in my statement, in my written statement prior to my testimony, these are only very general conclusions, and I'm very sorry that no further information has been included in these reports, including toxicological analysis, including ballistic analysis, and including detailed description of the entrance and exit wounds. So these are just very general conclusions. And I haven't had time now to see through them, but I can't find in the first two, and if I go further, three, so I can't find any reference to the military status of individual victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore, in those reports, as I was saying, we can see that 23 individuals had characteristic boots made in Austria. They had the same type of underclothes on, and the results --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've said all that. Let the witness deal with it. Have you seen these reports which are being referred to from various professors; Dunjic, Dobricanin, and Tasic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I help? I'm pretty sure she wouldn't have done there. As the accused has said, they were actually statements taken from those people by OTP investigators. The witness is, I think, referring to the source material for the reports that were prepared at the time. It's a document I referred to just before the break. They're available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've got these statements available.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: They are available. But I press no solution on the Court. A time may come when the Court would want the witness to see them in full, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think, since they're being referred to, she should have the opportunity to see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And we should have copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I wonder if some summary of that report is included in Defence Exhibit 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not sure about that. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Something went wrong with the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We have two available. The third is on its way. Dobricanin and Dunjic are here. I'm not, may I say at once, proposing or inviting the Court to admit them as evidence. They aren't witnesses we would necessarily rely on and have certainly made no effort to call, but statements were nevertheless taken from them and served on the accused in accordance with our duties of disclosure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Dr. Ranta, just have a brief look at those two, if you would.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, while the witness is looking at the reports, let me make use of the time. Mr. Nice said that they had no intention of tendering these documents as evidence, for obvious reasons and that is the reports show that these people were not civilians but members of the KLA, using firearms. And I ask that these three statements taken by the other side be tendered into evidence during this cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Our usual rule and one which I would have thought applied here is that we do not admit witness statements unless under particular rules. If you want in due course to call these witnesses to give their evidence, of course you can do so. But uncross-examined material is not usually admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Then let us proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two copies of the statement of Tasic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have here Dunjic's, Tasic's, and Dobricanin's statement to which I referred.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but it would take much longer to read through these witness information sheets. They contain a lot of information which of course is familiar to me, but to answer any questions put forward by the accused based on these is, unfortunately, impossible for me just by short reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Let us see whether there are any other questions about them and see if you can answer them or not. Mr. Milosevic, is there anything else you want to ask about the statements?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everything is in the statements. They speak for themselves. If I go into details, you will deny me the time. But in Dunjic's report, for example, it says these military boots on 23 persons. As you can see, they were not able to take these boots off because had they removed the footwear because of religious custom, they would have removed the footwear of all the persons. But they removed only the footwear of those wearing military boots. They were unable to take off the underwear showing their military status.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Now, we are not going to admit these statements. They are not evidence. They become evidence if the witness comes here and is cross-examined. Now, that has been, throughout, our ruling. The only circumstances in which we will admit a statement are, first of all, if it's admissible under the Rules, particularly 92 bis, and secondly, if there is an agreement or waiver on both sides that the document should be admitted. These have not been subject of such a waiver. They will not be admitted. You can call the witnesses when it comes to your case, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you. We ought to consider the time. You've now had well over the time. Let me just consider.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll give you another 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is not enough, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, just concentrate on what it is that you want to put. Concentrate on your main points and let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is my main point: For example, the witness herself said here what it says in the reports that I've mentioned, which you won't accept, but you will accept what the witness herself said, that the Serbian investigators carried out the paraffin test. It says here that out of 40 of them, 37, according to that test, had used firearms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You could put that. Just a moment. She's given evidence about the test, but of course you can put something to her.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Ranta, do you know that the paraffin test is officially used in Yugoslavia, and not only in Yugoslavia but in many other countries as well?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: I already said at the very beginning today that this was the first time ever I came across the use of paraffin test in reality, in practice. I was aware of this test but only as an historical test which is always mentioned in the textbooks. If this test is still in use in Yugoslavia, I strongly recommend the forensic investigators to adopt more specific and reliable tests. And I wish to emphasise also that, according to common internationally recognised procedures, the gunshot residue test should be taken within 3 to 6 hours after the alleged firing or use of firearms. To my understanding, if these paraffin casts were taken, they could have been taken on Monday, that is two days after the recovery of the bodies, which already is too late.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So much the greater value of the findings, because gunpowder residues were found on the hands of 37 out of 40 of those killed. Isn't that correct, Mrs. Ranta?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: To be precise --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That doesn't reflect what the statements say, if he's quoting from the statements. The Chamber -- I don't think the Chamber has --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've given them back, but what does it actually say?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, it's made clear that this is a nonspecific and old method of indicating gunpowder. It goes on to say that finding of nitrates, which is what this test reveals, on anyone is a nonspecific method and does not mean that gunpowder was present. It's on page 9 of 14 in Dobricanin, and it's possibly also worth observing, in light of what the witness has said, that Dobricanin makes it clear that these conclusions were not added to their own findings. These findings, I beg your pardon, weren't added to their written conclusions, he said, because they didn't have time. But it's all in this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Very well. But nonetheless, the accused is entitled to put his case to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Ranta, you say that the test can be of doubtful quality because it was done two days later, but you drew conclusions on the basis of an investigation, one of which was carried eight months later and another 14 months after the events in Racak. And in the meantime, the place had not been guarded and nobody knows what happened there. Isn't it correct that the first investigation that you know of was carried out only in November and the second one a few months after that?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: Now, I'm sorry to say that the accused is confusing issues that are irrelevant to each other. If we are talking about the gunpowder residue analysis, as the accused started, so I wish to emphasise once more that this test is unspecific for gunshot residue. It can show the presence of any oxidizing agent but it is not specific to nitrocellulose. So any oxidizing agent can give a positive reaction when paraffin and subsequently the diphenylamine dye is added. That for the first part. When I'm talking, or when we move to the scene investigations which were conducted, as the accused pointed out, yes, several months after the recovery of the bodies, we are talking about quite different type of investigations. We are talking about surveying the area where the bodies were recovered. I would imagine that this wouldn't have changed Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. too much. We are also dealing with forensic evidence which was detected under the surface of the soil, evidence which included bullets, bullet fragments, cartridge cases, human material. This is very different to gunshot residue analysis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, let's speed things up. We'll come to this. But do you agree with what your colleague Juha Rainino wrote in his Ph.D. dissertation where he says, in connection with Racak, that the answer to many questions lies in the realm of politics and that no answers can be expected from forensics experts? This is on page 94 of his thesis, which I have here. So despite some expectations, the political key question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Who is this gentleman you're referring to? A Ph.D. student, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Juha Rainino, Department of Forensic Medicine, University of Helsinki, Finland.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And when -- when are we talking about for the date of this -- have you got a date for this dissertation?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Helsinki 2002, academic dissertation approved by the faculty of medicine, University of Helsinki, to be presented for public discussion in the auditorium of the department of forensic medicine of the University of Helsinki at 12 noon 4th of October, 2002. Juha Rainino.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this dissertation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm very well aware of this because Dr. Juha Rainino was one of the members of the European Union forensic expert team, and I'm a co-author in most of the articles published in that Ph.D. thesis, so I'm very familiar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's why I'm asking you. My question is: Do you agree with his position? I do not consider it disputable that this is the doctor that this is known to the witness, but he says: "So despite some expectations, the political key question of the Racak incident could not be answered on the basis of the autopsy findings. Any attempt to do so would have revealed weak judgements."

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: I think this has already been made clear during this cross-examination, that forensic evidence as such has nothing to do with politics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. But the doctors from the Finnish team published a professional article. You know about this article, I hope. Juha Rainino, Dobricanin, and Penttila, [In English] Department of Forensic Medicine, University Helsinki.

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that. If I remember correctly, it's one of the first papers in the thesis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's been produced here. I think, if it's the same one, it's Exhibit D2, which we've marked for identification only. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just let me quote on page 8 of their article. They say: "Determinations [In English] for events, their political and moral meanings or the connection of victim to political or other organisations are questions which lie beyond the scope of forensic science. This should be realised by the authorities and also by the forensic scientists themselves." [Interpretation] I hope that this is not in dispute.

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: Before we go any further, Defence Exhibit 2 marked for identification is an article by Professor Dobricanin and his co-workers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be there's an error. It may be that there's a different article being referred to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Determinations for events --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. You've read that part out. What do you want the witness to answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So as far as I understand it, on the basis of your analysis, it cannot be established, and you cannot claim that these were civilians.

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't have the article which the accused is referring to. But I recognise the wording, "this should be realised by the authorities and also by the forensic scientists themselves" because this is the discussion we have been running at our department.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Since your main claim is that these people were shot there, did I understand this correctly, that they were executed? The spot.

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: I never used the word "executed." I have always said that they -- they were most probably killed where found. And this was the text from the press release on 17 March, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. But if there was -- please let me draw your attention to the same article, page 5.

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't have this article.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'll quote the sentence to you and you will remember it, and then you can either confirm or reject what it says here. I'm quoting from the article. The title is graphic table 4, Combination of Gunshot Injuries. "The number of gunshot wounds --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think if you're going to put this, the witness must have a copy of what you're putting, and we don't seem to have got it here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm just reading out the sentence, and the witness will certainly recall it. She must have read this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, she can't possibly recall everything that's said. She's entitled to have the document in front of her. You can read it out and then you can put it to her.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. I just wanted to read this first and then I will give it to the witness. There's no problem. It says here: [In English] [Previous translation continues]... gunshot wounds varied between 1 and 20. [Interpretation] Number of gunshot wounds varied between 1 and 20. One wound was found in six cases, and over 16 wounds in two cases." Mrs. Ranta, does this indicate that there was a battle there? Someone was hit with one bullet, somebody else with 16? This could not have been any kind of execution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before you answer, you'd better see the document. Mr. Milosevic, let the witness see the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just add that it says here, [In English] [Previous translation continues]... "analysis could not be carried out by UFET." That is your team. [Interpretation] Well, look here. Look at this report here. I hope you will recognise it. I have even marked some of the quotations or, rather, all the ones I've read, and there are some that I haven't had time to read out, but I have to save time.

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: As an answer to your question concerning the number of gunshot wounds, so this is just repetition from the autopsy reports. And the autopsy reports, as I have pointed out earlier, does not give enough evidence to answer the question of the circumstances around the death of these people. It only tells how they died. But they had been fired. Not about the circumstances around death.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There was another passage which the accused referred to, "analysis could not be carried out by the EU team." He may have marked the passages for your comment. If you can't find it, just say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This article is restricted to the autopsy findings, and detailed ballistic analysis could not be carried out by the European Union forensic expert team, yes, that is true. During the autopsies, the access of my investigators to any forensic material discovered and removed during the autopsies was restricted to the forensic investigators from the District Court of Pristina. So we were not able to take high-quality photographs, for instance, of all the bullets. And that makes it very difficult to compare the photographs taken during the autopsies with the photographs taken then of the forensic material recovered during the scene investigations. But, as I have pointed out in my statement, there were -- there was one photograph which could be compared from the autopsies with identified landmarks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you now, Mrs. Ranta, to look - and let's put it on the ELMO - a passage from your colleague's thesis showing the angles at which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Return the article to the accused and we'll see what the next point is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look at all the angles. From above, from below, from the front, from all sorts of angles that these people were hit. And doesn't this show that these people were shot in battle? Does this show this or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is no need to show me these because I have given instructions how these should be produced with the use of computer programmes. So I'm very familiar with what. And this -- the question as to the angles, so I think it's quite clearly stated in the article already, that without any further information about the circumstances around death, the categorisation of death is not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the categorisation of the circumstances of death is not possible based on a forensic analysis. Is this what you said? Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: The categorisation of manner of death as defined by the World Health Organisation is not possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Return that to the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke of a scene investigation which was carried out many months later and on the basis of which you produced a report, your new final report. Was this investigation attended by forensic archaeologists in order to determine whether the terrain had been changed, whether earth had been brought there or dug up and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: This scene investigation, which was conducted in November 1999, was planned to investigate different hypotheses around the death of these people which we have been discussing about. For us as a scientific team, it doesn't -- it wasn't important whether we found something, because the absence of evidence would also have been important. It is the question of systematic approach by excluding one hypothesis after another. I didn't think of forensic archaeologists particularly at the time of scene investigations, because we were still working as a European Union forensic expert team. And at the time we did these investigations, we had no forensic archaeologist on our team either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. That's what I asked you. So the scene investigation-- that is to say the incident took place in January, the scene investigation was in November, that makes it exactly ten months. Do you know that nobody provided security for the terrain during those ten months and that therefore nobody can guarantee that where you conducted your investigations was the same scene that existed at the time the incident took place? Would that be true, Mrs. Ranta?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: We had the opportunity of comparing photographic evidence from the site of recovery of the bodies in January 1999 to the scene investigations conducted in November.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, as we've cleared that point up, tell me this, please: On page 9, under J of your statement, you speak about traces on site which were found after the soil and surroundings were investigated. That means ten months later. So ten months later, you found something that you did not see on the first day or, rather, the bodies weren't seen on the first day either, it was only when Walker arrived with 30 journalists. But what was not found on that first day was found ten months later. Is it true that you in fact with those traces and remnants are dealing in a field for which you were not competent, because this is work reserved for ballistics and forensic archaeologists exclusively and professionals close to that field of expertise?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't quite catch the point. I wish to refer to the report from scene investigations, and particularly page 9 in the report of scene investigations which were submitted to the Tribunal. And I understand that this has been filed as evidence in this case. Am I correct, Mr. Prosecutor? Yes. So instead of referring --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's been filed. We'll find it for you, and the tab reference. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But my question then is as follows: In view of the fact that this is not part of your job, it is a job for ballistics and forensic archaeologists, how come you claim that they are civilians? Where did you get the freedom to do so? And that the place of the killing was actually the gully? You even state that people were killed close, too, at close range. How are you able to claim that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think the witness has answered the question. Is there anything you want to add? We've been over this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I hope that Mr. Prosecutor would be able to produce the document I wish to refer, because it has been filed as evidence in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think it's tab 12 of binder 2 of Exhibit 156. But since the witness hadn't got so far to as say as what it was she was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was referring to page 9, scene investigation in November 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. That's the correct document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Has she got that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have, yes. I have my own copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You have it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have my own copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have copies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wish to emphasise the list of participants. Myself in the capacity of a team leader and the presence of altogether six forensic investigators. One senior investigator and then five individual investigators, and their special expertise is quoted there. We had an expert on topography. That is the surveying of the terrain. We had an expert on documentation. Finally, we had an expert on ballistics and two additional for documentation. And this was a team that we considered appropriate to conduct scene investigations. To include a forensic archaeologist, I don't think that it would have brought any additional value to this investigation, particularly which I have totally forgotten to include in my curriculum vitae is that in fact I have participated during three summers also archaeological excavations in Finland.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, all right. Mrs. Ranta, could you answer the next question: If the projectiles were found under suspicious conditions ten months later, let it be said, near a body or immediately underneath a corpse, does that then imply that those persons were in a lying-down position or, rather, in combat position, which further indicates that they had been killed in combat? How else would the projectiles have been found underneath their bodies? My question is the following, actually: Is it impossible that the projectiles and parts of projectiles were to be found underneath the bodies or immediately around them if they had been shot standing up? Because the projectiles passing through the bodies would continue their trajectory through their propulsory motion and therefore would be found quite a long way away from the body, very often quite a long way away unless they are stopped by any obstacle. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: This question would require about a lecture of four or five hours to answer -- to give a comprehensive answer. What I'm referring and emphasising once again is that we did not find the -- the bullets and bullet fragments under the bodies because we were not there when they were found. We are only referring to bullets and bullet fragments that were recovered underneath the surface of the ground. So -- and some -- and some of them taking and tearing off also human material with them. I find it extremely difficult to figure out how these bullets and bullet fragments could have penetrated the ground had they been fired in the distance of hundred or 200 metres. It's impossible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, your time is almost up. You've had nearly three-quarters of an hour longer than you were originally allotted, so you must finish in the next two minutes, and we'll then have the amici's questions and we'll adjourn.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is absolutely impossible for me to conclude my cross-examination in two minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You have two minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have several more very important questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: All right. Ask two of them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have -- I'll tell you. Let me just look it up. I have another 30 questions, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Pick the two most important ones.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't pick them, Mr. May, so I'll take them in their order, because I can't work in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned a number of cartridges near the bodies and ascribe them to the attackers. Isn't it more realistic that they might have belonged to people who were fighters themselves and who in that gully and on the edges of the gully, that they were in a sort of trench and waited in an ambush? How would the attackers have chargers or batches of the weapons? Isn't it more logical to ascribe this to that belonging to the people fighting there and who were killed on the spot?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: I have never referred to who -- who the perpetrators were and who had fired these weapons. All I have been saying is that we found forensic evidence in the form of bullets and bullet fragments and in the form of cartridge cases and that we were able to tell the origin of this ammunition and that human material was attached to some of the bullets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Ranta, you know full well that human tissue, once the bullet enters the ground, is cleaned by the ground and soil, and after eight months you couldn't have any human remains. That is quite nonsensical. But let me ask you this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. If you're putting that it's nonsensical to a scientist, you should put it clearly. Ms. Ranta, it is being suggested that what you're saying is nonsensical in this connection. Would you like to answer that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, Mr. May --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Let the witness answer. You'll get your extra question. Don't worry about that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wish to refer to my statement which has been submitted to all parties present here, submitted on 20 February 2003. And I'm referring to page 11 where I in detail describe the recovery of identifiable human material in the form of two mandibular molars in the vicinity of defined bullets under the surface of the ground in a position where victim RA-24-7021F was recovered in January. Also I refer to the post-mortem investigation of the victim, including both schematic presentation of the entrance and exit wounds and photographs taken by OSCE verifiers and during the autopsy. We were able to extract amplifiable DNA from one of the molars and the DNA was compared to that of the victim, and the DNA profiles did match. The other type of human material which I was referring to was soft tissue material, and we did all the efforts to extract identifiable DNA from that. And I have discussed this as well in my statement, telling that, unfortunately, we were not able to do that. And I also give some possible explanations to that. This, to my knowledge, is the first time ever that attempts like this have been conducted. Whether it's nonsense scientifically, I don't think that is a justified statement on that. I think scientifically, and a scientist has to try everything in his or her power to complete the task that has been entrusted to him or her, and this is what we did in this case. We know very well that the degradation of human tissue varies on different factors, including the humidity, including the variation in temperature, including the Ph value, the acidity of the soil, et cetera. But I think it was correct to try also with this partly degraded human soft tissue remnants, to try to extract DNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But you are speaking in principle about an attempt that proved fruitless; isn't that right? It was not successful.

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: It was not successful in that case. And I have also given explanations why it may have failed, and they are all scientific facts that I have given as explanation: The presence of enzyme inhibitors, no enzyme inhibitors in the bullets; the possibility of DNA destruction by the variation of temperature; and thirdly, the enzymic activity of the soil bacteria. They are all scientific facts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, we're not having a scientific discussion here, but very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, there is a judgement by the court in Pristina which tried a particular individual, and Judge Gajvan [phoen] took part, and Besim Kelmendi, the president of the council, Amnisa Bellart [phoen], and so on. This was an international construction of some kind, and I have the entire judgement here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But for you, Mrs. Ranta, a question: Are you aware of the forensic report that was handed over in that trial? Dr. Peter Markestein is the author of the report in that particular case, and very precisely in the judgement, 133 paragraph, it states that the exact distance of the firing of a shot cannot be ascertained. The exact range or distance was not able to be ascertained on the basis of the autopsy. And then he goes on to state, in paragraph 165 of the judgement, that court in Pristina assesses, and as you can see it was made up of judges of different nationalities, that Haris Bajrami, and Bestan Dositi [phoen], Nasmet Mahuti [phoen], those three men, that the bullets were shot by a group of policemen situated on a hill south of the area, that is to say, from a considerable distance. Now, this Dr. Peter Markestein, I don't know if you've heard of Dr. Peter Markestein. I have not myself, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it is very difficult to follow all this. Is this anything to do with Racak, first of all?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It does have to do with Racak because Mrs. Ranta claims in her report that the people were killed from close range, from close to. Whereas this judgement, which refers to Racak where a forensic expert once again, in this case Peter Markestein, gives precise assertions to the effect that the exact distance at which a shot was fired cannot be established. And for the three persons, the judgement on these three persons, that it was ascertained that a group of policemen had done the shooting and that they were situated up on a hilltop. So I'm presenting this to challenge the claim that they were killed at close range, close to. And I would like to support my claim that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just one thing at a time. This is a case, is it, which concerns the shooting at Racak? Can we understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. The judgement relates to it. It is the District Court in Pristina, and a case is being tried with respect to Racak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know anything about this, Dr. Ranta?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The original question of the accused was whether I was aware of this forensic report. I haven't seen it. I was aware that there was a trial at the District Court of Pristina. And as to the forensic expert quoted here, I also -- I have met him in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I suppose you haven't got -- have you got that in English or is it just in Serbian?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have it in Serbian, but I am sure that there is a copy in English, because it was foreign judges. So it must have been in English, because none of these foreigners knew Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you help with this one?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Not immediately. I can research the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Could you. We'll adjourn for 20 minutes. Mr. Milosevic, we'll give you time to clarify this matter. If possible, we'll get hold of the judgement and we'll see if it can be exhibited or not, if there is any objection to it be exhibited. We will then give you another ten minutes because of the importance of this evidence to you, but beyond that we won't go. Mr. Tapuskovic, have you got any questions arising out of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think I'll be able to be of assistance to the Trial Chamber, if I might say so, to dwell on professional issues. So I should like to ask the Court's indulgence Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. and give me a little time, and I will try and be as brief as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We will adjourn now. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The transcript of the trial has been located. It's in English. Can I explain the position by reference to an exhibit that you already have, 94, tab 73. If I throw it on the overhead projector, you'll take the point immediately. The trial concerned the death -- and you'll remember this exhibit, it was shown through General Drewienkiewicz, I think. And I put on a red sticker. The sticker identifies the area of the gully. The victim in this murder trial's name was Hajrizi Bajrami, and you will remember that this map has a key running down the left-hand side, and beside the left-hand red sticker on the key you will see the name of this victim Hajrizi Bajrami, and the place where he was killed was not the gully at all. It's further down, below the red sticker, at site number 2, and I think it's number 3 of number 2. So that whatever the evidence that the accused is referring to relates to, it doesn't relate to anything in the gully. I have found -- or, rather, to be precise, those assisting me have, with great speed and efficiency, found not only the transcript but the evidence of Peter Markestein, and I think that's the person with whom we are concerned. I haven't yet located his report, and at the moment, on scanning the transcript of his evidence, I can't find a passage that relates to the topic asked of by the accused. I'll carry on looking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. You've got another 10 minutes. If there is anything more you want to ask about this, we can consider admitting the court record and the judgement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I quoted point 133 of the judgement, where it says that the exact distance was not able to be ascertained on the basis of the autopsy, the distance at which the shot was fired. And what Mr. Nice is talking about refers to point 165, where it says that it was from the Vrelo hill, to make things clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Ranta, as you're talking about firing at close range, and your colleague says that this cannot be ascertained, on page 13 of your own report, you speak of the following, and this in connection to the ammunition found during the investigations. This is contained in sub-item 8, I believe, on page 13 of your statement, and you say that Yugoslav manufacturers, and you mention IK (Igman Zavod Konjic), do you know that Konjic is to be located in Bosnia-Herzegovina and that Konjic is a town which was not under the control of Republika Srpska throughout the war and conflicts? And secondly, do you know that in different ways, among other ways, by looting and so on, members of the terrorist organisation, the KLA, came and used the ammunition which was produced by Yugoslavia, manufactured in Yugoslavia? So can we at all, on the basis of all this, claim that those shots were fired, bullets were fired by the Yugoslav or, rather, the Serb policemen on the basis of what you say, that the manufacturers of the ammunition that was found on the site were from IK manufacture -- manufactured by IK (Igman Zavod Konjic) and the Titova Uzice factory?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: In this point 8, I'm just stating that the manufacturers of the ammunition recovered, they originated from these two manufacturers. And looking in detail of the loading year or its approbation as pointed out in the head stamp of each cartridge case, they -- there's a wide range of the loading years. So I'm not referring in any way to the war or were they during the war, anything like that. This is just the way the ballistics expert already referred to earlier wrote the report which has been submitted to this Tribunal as an annex to our results from the scene investigations. As to the precise location of these factories of these manufacturers, I haven't made any effort to localise them. And I'm not drawing any conclusions as to who fired the shots. I have never indicated the perpetrator or perpetrators in any of these cases, because it would have been -- such a comment would have been inappropriate, because we were not mandated to investigate the question of guilt, we were only mandated to investigate the death of people who were found killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Fine. Now, tell me, in view of the fact that this is a question which relates to your profession directly, how do you explain the following phenomenon: That some bodies were found in that gully, the one you mention, and that they were leaning with their backs on the ground and their hands and legs were partially raised in a bent position? They were up in the air. How do you explain that? Doesn't that indicate that the bodies were brought in from somewhere else and placed at that scene? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: I'm only referring to the photographic evidence as documented by the OSCE on the day of the recovery of the bodies. And this has been the basis of our documentation. I have not commented on the position of the bodies in any other relation but the possibility of turning over the bodies so that the faces would be exposed. That's all I have said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But they say that on the spot -- or, rather, that the findings from the scene and projectiles were compared to photographs carried out and made by the Finnish experts during the autopsy; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: We combined the photographs of the OSCE, and that was the basis of the scene investigations, and we had our own autopsy reports so that the bullet paths could be compared based on that, that's all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But I assume you know, because you're a forensic expert, that there are no photographs which can be used in the sense of ballistic comparison and correlation and identification of bullets, of projectiles and weapons.

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: The photographs made by OSCE were used to localise, to give the approximate location of each body at the time of the recovery of the bodies. And when we did conduct our scene investigations, the area which we covered by metal detectors and by surveying the terrain was much larger, being some 170 metres in length. And if we think about the recovery of the bodies at the gully, they were found at the length of some 65 metres, if I remember correctly. The width of the area we covered varied from 30 to 60 metres, depending on the elevations at the gully.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And were you -- do you know about the findings of the ballistics experts mentioned in the judgement I quoted a moment ago? And that is paragraph 140, or item 140. That's where that is contained. And they say that individual injuries could even have occurred from ricochetted bullets and could cause injury on those bodies of the type that existed.

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: If we are thinking about the quality of the ground and the soil at the gully, there is really a danger for ricochetting. About the results from the scene investigations, I wish to emphasise that we are only talking about the bullets and bullet fragments that were discovered underneath the surface of the ground, sometimes having human material attached to that. I don't think that ricochetting could occur in that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But a moment ago I understood you to say that you did not establish that it was human tissue but that you attempted, as a scientific challenge, to arrive at that result but that the attempt was unsuccessful. That's what I understood you to say. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: The attempt to extract amplifiable DNA for DNA profiling was unsuccessful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you must now bring this examination to a close. You can ask two more questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Mr. May. I'm going to ask you one question first. Because Mrs. Ranta built into her report, to her findings, the results of those subsequent on-site investigations that took place eight and 14 months later, and reports on those investigations is something that I do not have, I haven't been given them, could you please tell me, as Mrs. Ranta did incorporate them into her report, when will I be given a chance to cross-examine the witness about those particular reports, that is to say the reports she incorporated into her report? Or if I cannot cross-examine her, who should I cross-examine with respect to these subsequent investigations, that is to say the ones taken -- carried out 10 and 14 months later?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mrs. Ranta, have we got all the reports which you made? Have they all be turned handed over to the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have handed over the report of scene investigations conducted in November 1999 and in March 2000, and these are the results which I have been referring to in my written statement which I have submitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. And all the documents have been exhibited or disclosed. May we be sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Binder 2, tab 12, is headed "Report of Scene Investigations in November 1999 and in March 2000."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is Exhibit 156.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's been exhibited. It's been exhibited for some time. Now, if you want to ask the witness two more questions, you can, Mr. Milosevic. You will then have had two hours and more in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but as the witness, Mr. May, did not take part in those scene investigations, who is it who I'm able to cross-examine with respect to those reports?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If there is some matter you wish to cross-examine about, you may make an application to us and we'll look at it, we'll consider it. But let us finish our examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Ranta, you said in your report that the people involved here were civilians. I have a photograph here. Do you know how the KLA marked the grave of one of those, as you call them, civilians? Here it is clearly seen that it was a member of the KLA, and the tombstone of that person, their member who was killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness cannot answer that unless -- Have you been to a cemetery? Have you seen these graves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have visited Racak -- the cemetery which is close to the village, in 2001, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, then let the witness -- let the witness see what it is you want to show.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can see it too and the witness can be shown it as well. It can be placed on the overhead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, let us see it. What is it supposed to represent, so we understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It represents the grave of that KLA fighter who was killed in Racak and which the KLA visibly marked with its own insignia and signs and his name and the date of death, the 15th of January. So those are one of those civilians, as they claim that they were civilians or, rather, unarmed persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I have no doubt we can in fact track this down because it's not disputed that there were some KLA members killed, but not, of course, that they were in the gully. We will see -- we will see what the witness says. Can you help us with that at all, Dr. Ranta?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I haven't seen this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You haven't.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I haven't. But, Your Honour, may I add something? The accused said that since I did not participate the scene investigations. I did participate both scene investigations, in November 1999 and in March 2000, and I had planned them together with my investigators.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Hand the photograph back. Yes. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. It is very difficult to focus on professional issues alone, but I'll do my best. Questioned by Mr. Tapuskovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Ranta, in your brief CV, you state some things related to your expertise and expert knowledge. And as I can see here, you're a doctor of dentistry, that you were the mentor of five dissertations, microbiology and other subjects as well; is that right? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you just tell me, please, whether you had expert papers or expert knowledge in the field of criminal science, ballistics, or forensic medicine, legal?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: I have publications both in forensic odontology, in forensic medicine, in ballistics without being an expert on ballistics. And it has already been -- some of the publications where I'm a co-author have been included and discussed here today. In addition to that, I have also published other scientific papers which cover my expertise in connective tissue diseases, molecular biology, microbiology, electromicroscopy, and some also in international humanitarian law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. According to your statement, the one we're discussing here today and the one you're stating your views on, you dealt first and foremost in teamwork, equipment, negotiations, and the necessary security measures involved. That's what your work entailed as well; right?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: As a team leader, I had a very great variety of tasks during this investigation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I understand. However, I see from your report specifically as you write here, the representatives of the European Union at no point issued any instructions or authorisation for more detailed criminal investigation. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it also correct that on 30th of January, 1999, some 15 days after the event took place, that you asked for authorisation from the Yugoslav authorities to go to the site but that you were prevented from doing so by the snow? Otherwise, that there were no other obstacles.

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: The team members visited the village of Racak on Saturday, and that must have been the 30th, yes. January 30 in 1999. And as I pointed out earlier, yes, it had been snowing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's why you couldn't do your job there?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: It was physically impossible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In your report of the 17th of March, 1999, which has already been discussed here, you say the following, and do you agree that that is what you said then: "The first key move that would normally be expected in any crime scene," as you say, "would be the isolation of the area and the exclusion of unauthorised access. The scene should then be photographed and videotaped, any evidence be collected, and victims localised and marked at site. This step should also include sampling for gunshot residue and so on. Because this was not done, important information at the site may have been lost." Do you agree with this in view of the fact that not everything that should have been done was done on the spot, that this could have led to loss of very important information?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: As I said, important information at the site may have been lost. That's all I said, and I -- I still adhere to this comment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, in view of this, my time is very limited so I will show you only a few photographs. This is from the Prosecution documents, tab number 6, Racak number 1, where you can see 12 persons who lost their lives. If you would please look at this photograph and then I will put a question to you in connection with it. Have you ever seen this photograph before?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: Again, I wish to emphasise that I have seen so many photographs of this particular scene. Whether this is exactly the same which I have seen, I can't tell you, but I recognise all the bodies that are exhibited here from the gully. I have a recollection that I haven't seen the people standing behind there at the top of the page. I probably have only see a photograph with the legs. But otherwise, yes, this is familiar to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is the following: These are bodies photographed on that day on the spot. After the bodies were lifted up and if only the place had been photographed, would we now be able to say, because of the blood traces, that there is no doubt that this is where these people bled to death? If you look at the photograph, you can see no traces of blood around the bodies lying there.

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: Your Honour, just by looking at the photograph of this quality, I don't want to make any conclusions or any suggestions as to the presence or absence of blood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you misunderstood me. What I'm trying to say is the following: This photograph is something on the basis of which, if the indictment is correct, some 12 people lost their lives. After the corpses were lifted up on that day, after the representatives of the OSCE had been there, had the place been photographed and all of them had been hit with at least four or five bodies [as interpreted], would we be able to see the situation underneath the bodies? But this was not done.

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: We are coming to the shortcomings of the initial steps in the investigations, and I have also pointed out the problem that the bodies were not documented at the site and given individual numbers and that they were not then packed in individual body bags. Had there been police officers at site, had there been exclusion of unauthorised access, anything is possible, but today here, I can't say yes, probably the photographs would show the presence or absence of blood. What I would like to say in this connection is this is only photograph, and there are several photographs which can be examined, photographs that are of better quality, and there the possibility of blood or its absence can be confirmed. One of the reasons why I sent my investigators to Racak when we had completed the autopsies was to go to the gully and, if possible, take soil samples. Because those soil samples, remembering that it was cold, could have been used for at least an attempt, a scientific attempt to extract amplifiable DNA and possibly compare the DNA profiles with those which were performed during the autopsies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One more question in this connection, and if you can answer, please do so. If you can't, then please say so. There are 12 bodies here of people who lost their lives. There's no blood around. You know how human blood behaves when people are hit with many bullets. You can see no traces of blood around here, and blood should have spattered all over the place. There should have been traces of blood on the bodies. Can you answer this or not?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: Sir, I would like to refer to the autopsy reports where there's detailed documentation of clothing of these people, showing plenty of coagulated blood. If we go back to the fact that these people were wearing several warm jackets, the fact that there are no spillings to be seen here is, I think, quite natural. And as I said, this can be verified from each individual autopsy protocol of these 12 people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. But please, maybe you misunderstood me, but thank you. What I would especially like to draw attention to with these questions, and I think this would be very useful to the Chamber, and all of this is in 1L, paragraph 1L of your report consisting of eight points, after which you conclude that these are matters of fact. And if we start from item 1, you say that there is a connection between the body and the bullet, as you say. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: Starting from point 1, you're referring to page 11 in my statement, I assume. I'm saying that the two mandibular molars, they were recovered in the vicinity of three bullets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I fully agree. This is very precise, and I accept this. I have no comment on this. But in this case, you were able to prove that this man lost his life on that spot; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: As stated later in this paper. So I just look at the precise wording here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just please confirm that this is correct. That's all I'm asking you. I'm not challenging what you established here.

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: I have stated that this particular victim had been shot at the gully, bearing in mind that the wounds were inflicted during lifetime or when the people were still alive or at around death.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But in item 2, you are embarking on an assumption. You are comparing the bullet recovered in the body of the man who lost his life and the bodies later found during the scene investigation. So there is no direct link between the bullets found in the body and the bullet found much later on. So the bullet is similar to the bullets found later.

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: This detailed information is included in the report of scene investigations which has been filed as evidence in this case, and it is Annex 6, entitled "Comparative Ballistics." As I already pointed out earlier, the chain of custody of the bullets during the autopsies was restricted to the investigating judge or, more precisely, to forensic investigators from her office. So we were only able to take photographs of the bullets. Those bullets which we recovered --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Ranta, I'm not challenging what you established. Please. I have to bear in mind the time. What I'm saying is that you did not establish a direct link here between the bullets found later on the scene but in the bullet recovered from the body. This was done only indirectly. The bullets were similar. Is this correct or not?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: The bullets bore identical landmarks and identifiable landmarks, and this comparison was made by expert on ballistics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's what I'm asking you. I'm just asking you to confirm this. So in two cases, you drew this kind of comparison. Then we come to points 3, 4, and 5, and these again are connected to assumptions of yours. Now we have two persons, and we can no longer say that you were able to establish a direct link between the bullet recovered from the bodies and the traces found on the scene.

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: Excuse me, are you referring to point 3? This is about the vitality of the wounds? Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not challenging this, no. But from this, we cannot see anything specific linked to someone who might have lost his life on that spot except that the wounds were received during the person's lifetime.

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: This is a general finding from the autopsies and refers also to one of the hypotheses which we have discussed today, and that was the possibility of the scene being set up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And 4 and 5 are also points linked to hypotheses; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: Points 4 and 5 state just that we can look at the distribution of bullets and bullet fragments recovered in November 1999, and in point 5 that we can look at the distribution of cartridge cases recovered at the gully. This is just the result of our investigations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, now, all these questions were put to you because I wanted to ask you something about point 6 and 7. This refers to people who lost their lives in the village. They have nothing to do with the gully. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are these the three persons we can see in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: The answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now look at photograph number 2. They're all together on this photograph. But on this other photograph they are marked precisely with the numbers you have in your report, and here they are separated with quite a distance between each corpse. Are these the same three persons here?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: To my vision, yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you explain, then, this sort of movement or shift? You said in your report that there were no traces of any -- any setup, as you said.

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: Your Honour, the photograph which was first shown to me - I'm referring to this one - is the one which we have used in our documentation and also in our subsequent scene investigations. And this same scene is theoretically presented here, having these three victims with the sternum as a reference point located exactly at these sites.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Any question of trying to set that scene up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's quite clear that the body at the top must have been moved at one stage. I don't know who has taken this photograph. And as I said, we have used the photograph which was first shown to me as our reference, because this is the OSCE documentation which was handed over to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In any event, this is not the gully. This is somewhere else in the village.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In fact, this is close -- very close to the village, but it's not inside the village itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next point you explained here concerns the time when these people may have lost their lives, and you said it was approximately at the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. same time. But in your report, you wrote in your report of the 17th of March, 1999, the most that can be said is that it seems that the victims died at approximately the same time. At approximately the same time.

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you said this then, can you now answer my question, in view of the time when the autopsies were carried out, the most that can be said that they lost their lives at approximately the same time, what would that mean? Within a few hours of each other? On the same day? Can you approximate this time span?

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will be quick, but I have to go back to a question. And if you will allow me, I would like to tell you something that has to do with the practice before the Yugoslav courts in the cases of blood crimes. Allow me to say that I have been a lawyer -- an attorney-at-law for 40 years and that I have participated in hundreds of murder cases as Defence counsel, and we have never had a case in which a paraffin cast was not made. When the paraffin cast is made, this is considered to be indisputable evidence that the accused perpetrated the murder.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I would like to ask you, although in other places paraffin casts are no longer used, if the most eminent experts of Yugoslav forensic science told you that they took paraffin casts and that in 37 out of 40 cases there were traces of gunpowder particles on the hands, why didn't you deal with this problem and introduce it into your report in some way? Because this was said by people who are sworn expert witnesses in courts.

utterances.speaker: HELENA RANTA
utterances.text: We have discussed about the gunshot residue analysis here in quite a lengthy way. I have referred to textbooks, and as I said, I was very surprised to meet people and to hear that the paraffin casts were in use. As you, sir, have pointed out, it has been used and it is still in use in Yugoslavia. It is a method, as I said, of no scientific value, and I'm referring to modern textbooks.
